caption:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei answered a safety critic with a post of nearly 2,000 words on X.
He listed decisions he says cost Anthropic money, like holding back its Mythos-class models for months.
He also admitted mistakes and promised options for regulating the pace of AI research by January 15, 2027.

Is Anthropic really the safety-first AI company?

paragraphs.text: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei published a post of nearly 2,000 words on X on October 20, 2026, responding to criticism from Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer of the AI safety nonprofit Encode. Calvin had accused Anthropic of undermining its safety commitments. According to The Next Web, the post had been viewed more than 800,000 times by October 21.

Calvin's criticism followed the backlash over a leaked draft of a federal AI safety bill from Anthropic. On October 19, Calvin wrote that Anthropic's response to that backlash was still not engaging with the central issue, according to The Next Web. BigGo Finance reported that Calvin listed nine Anthropic actions that he said undercut the company's stated safety goals.

In reply, Amodei described the company's approach as a race to the top, the idea that building the technology responsibly at the frontier can raise standards across the industry. He said the strategy only works if the company following it stays at the frontier, and he listed nine decisions that he said cost Anthropic commercially but improved safety.

The most prominent example was the company's Mythos-class models. Amodei said Anthropic had trained them by February 2026 but did not make them generally available until June, after stronger cyber safeguards were in place. In the meantime, only a small group of cyber defense partners had access. He wrote that the company likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead.

He also pointed to biological safeguards strict enough that, he said, biologists joke about them, and said Anthropic had seen and blocked possible attempts to use its models for bioweapons. BigGo Finance reported that the filters sometimes misread intent and routed some users to less capable models, and that an August update cut such fallbacks by about 85% in company testing.

On China, Amodei wrote that Anthropic was the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to companies controlled by the People's Republic of China. He also cited Anthropic's support for California's SB 53, a June call for government authority to block model releases, support for chip export controls, and a public benefit fund set to hold 5% of the company's shares.

Amodei acknowledged that the company had made mistakes, including how it communicated about the draft federal AI safety bill, Fox News reported. The Next Web reported that he said Anthropic could have handled three of Calvin's points better, attributing the problems to rhetoric or policy communication that was not carefully written inside a company of more than 5,000 people. He wrote that he is the chief executive and takes responsibility.

He called Calvin's point about changes to the Responsible Scaling Policy, Anthropic's internal safety rulebook, the most substantive item, and said the earlier version had been too rigid. He also said the company is nearing a point where AI progress moves faster than safety work can keep up. According to Fox News, Anthropic committed to proposing options for regulating the pace of AI research by January 15, 2027, or to explaining why it will not.

Not everyone was persuaded. Sigal Samuel of Vox asked Amodei for evidence that the strategy works, writing that from the outside Anthropic appeared to have done more on net to drive a race to the bottom, The Next Web reported.

The exchange arrives at a sensitive moment for Anthropic, which is preparing for a public listing and is under closer scrutiny of how its safety claims match its commercial behavior. By naming specific decisions and dates, Amodei turned a broad argument about intentions into a list of claims that outside critics can check, and by setting a January 15 date he gave them a clear marker to hold the company to.
The next test is whether Anthropic publishes concrete options for regulating the pace of AI research by January 15, 2027, and whether those options would limit its own development.
